data.title: Live updates: Trump sets up Medicaid drug price reductions; Vance stumps in Iowa with blistering attack on Dems
data.description:
The Midwest is home to several contentious congressional and gubernatorial races in November, historically red areas that are seeing Democratic candidates make inroads.

Vice President Vance visited one of them for a rally on Friday: Council Bluffs, Iowa. He was joined by Republican gubernatorial candidate Zach Lahn, who is running against Democratic state Auditor Rob Sand. Vance laid into Sand for more than five minutes at the rally.

The rally’s location is the turf of Democratic Senate candidate Josh Turek, who is campaigning against Rep. Ashley Hinson (R-Iowa) for the open seat. Hinson reportedly won’t attend the Vance event.

In Kansas, Adam Hamilton (D) narrowly leads Republican Sen. Roger Marshall in a tight race for Senate, according a The Hill/Emerson College poll out Friday. It found Hamilton ahead by 2 percentage points, with 45 percent support to Marshall’s 43 percent.

The Pentagon told congressional leaders this week that the cost of the Iran war through Sept. 3 had exceeded $43 billion, not including damage estimates to sites hit.

At the White House, President Trump will make an announcement about Medicaid drug prices Friday afternoon. He’ll hold other meetings and will head Friday evening to his golf course in Sterling, Va., for a MAGA Inc. meeting. He’ll spend part of the weekend at Camp David.

Follow live below.

data.title: Wendy's franchisee with hundreds of locations across 15 states files for bankruptcy
data.description:
(NEXSTAR) – A Wendy’s franchisee that operates 314 of the fast food company’s restaurants in 15 states announced Friday that it will be filing for bankruptcy.

Meritage Hospitality Group, headquartered in Grand Rapids, Michigan, announced in a news release that it was voluntarily filing for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in a bid to, in part, “strengthen its balance sheet.”

The news comes months after the company announced it would close 60 locations to boost its performance in 2026.

Meritage also owns one Bojangles and five “independently branded concepts,” but those ventures were not enough to offset the financial struggles of its Wendy’s stores.

“Because the substantial majority of Meritage’s restaurant portfolio operates under Wendy’s brand, those system-wide pressures have had a significant impact on the Company’s financial position,” the company said in the release.

Amid soaring beef costs, Wendy’s has reported same-store sales losses for six straight quarters, CNBC reports.

Meritage owns Wendy’s locations in Arkansas, Connecticut, Florida, Georgia, Indiana, Massachusetts, Michigan, Missouri, Mississippi, North Carolina, Ohio, Oklahoma, Tennessee, Texas, and Virginia.

The company, which made no mention of any closure plans, says it anticipates maintaining normal restaurant operations during the restructuring process, and “will continue to serve guests every day, and its team members remain the heart of this business.”

Nexstar reached out to Wendy’s corporate team for a statement, but did not immediately receive a response.

data.title: 43 percent say Trump responsible for current state of economy: Survey
data.description:
A large share of Americans say President Trump is to blame for the current economic conditions facing the nation, including high inflation and affordability concerns, according to a new survey.

The Politico/Public First poll, released Thursday, found that 43 percent of respondents believe the president is mostly or fully responsible for the state of the economy. The survey indicated a deep partisan split on the issue, with 19 percent of Republicans and 70 percent of Democrats holding Trump accountable.

Meanwhile, another 16 percent said they place equal blame on Trump and former President Biden, while 29 percent placed greater blame on the latter.

A majority of Americans in this survey rated concerns about the cost of living as the top issue facing the U.S. right now. About 27 percent ranked the “poor state” of the economy and 22 percent selected high taxes as the nation’s top problem. 

This new data comes as the Trump administration seeks to calm concerns about affordability ahead of the midterms and amid ongoing U.S. military operations against Iran, which have strained global energy supplies, and a tariff fight with Canada. 

The president has repeatedly blamed unfavorable economic reports on the Biden administration and claimed energy prices that have skyrocketed during the Iran war “will drop precipitously” when the monthslong conflict comes to a close. 

During a Wednesday campaign event in North Carolina, Trump told supporters that higher gas prices were a “very inexpensive price to pay” for these military operations. 

This week, regular unleaded gas jumped from a national average of $4.31 to $4.43 in the span of four days, according to AAA. The national average price of diesel jumped by 42 cents over the last week.  

The Politico poll was conducted from Sept. 13-15 across a sample of 2,064 Americans. The margin of error is around 2.2 percentage points.

data.title: Silicon Valley Bank failure review finds Fed staff 'should have known' about risks
data.description:
A new review of the Silicon Valley Bank collapse found Federal Reserve supervisory staff “knew or should have known” about the institution’s vulnerabilities, Michelle Bowman, the Fed’s vice chair for supervision, said Friday.

The initial findings from an outside consulting firm’s independent review suggested the biggest bank failure since the 2008 financial crisis resulted from poor management and a lack of “decisive action” by Fed supervisory staff.

It also determined that a 2018 law rolling back portions of the Dodd-Frank Act did not contribute to the central bank’s delayed response, breaking with a prior assessment from Bowman’s predecessor.

“Their report marks a pivotal moment not just in our understanding of what went wrong at SVB, but in our understanding of what went wrong within the Federal Reserve’s supervisory process,” Bowman said in prepared remarks from London.

“This review is not about assigning blame,” she added. “Instead, it is about learning lessons from the past to avoid repeating them in the future.”

Bowman asked the Starling Advisory Group to conduct a new investigation into the bank’s failure after she took over as vice chair for supervision last June.

They found that Silicon Valley Bank’s collapse in early 2023, which was quickly followed by the failures of both First Republic Bank and Signature Bank, was the result of a “confluence of vulnerabilities.”

The bank faced unrealized losses as the Fed hiked interest rates in 2022 and 2023, according to the review. Its reliance on uninsured deposits from venture capital-backed tech firms compounded the problem and left it at risk of a run.

Fed supervisory staff “knew, or should have known, about these vulnerabilities as early as March 2022” and failed to take “prompt and decisive action to encourage or require” the bank to reduce its risks, the review noted.

It added that delays in supervisory action were not the result of “the regulatory tailoring mandate” in a 2018 law that loosened key portions of the Dodd-Frank Act, which was passed in the wake of the 2008 financial crisis.

The review pointed to a “long-standing culture of risk aversion” among staff, who “believed it was personally safer to take no action unless they were certain the action was exactly right,” as well as confusion over who could decide on the right course of action.

Bowman’s predecessor, Michael Barr, issued an initial report on Silicon Valley Bank’s collapse in April 2023.

Barr, who still serves on the Fed board, similarly found that bank leaders failed to manage risks — while Fed supervisors did not “fully appreciate the extent” of the bank’s vulnerabilities or take sufficient steps to address these issues once they were identified.

However, his report also suggested that the 2018 rollback of portions of Dodd-Frank “impeded effective supervision by reducing standards, increasing complexity, and promoting a less assertive supervisory approach.”

data.title: Vance ends Iowa rally with seven-minute censure of Rob Sand
data.description:
Vice President Vance zeroed in on Iowa Democratic nominee Rob Sand during a rally in Council Bluffs on Friday, saying he is too far left to lead the state.

Rand is leading in several polls in the contest to succeed Gov. Kim Reynolds (R) in November. 

In a roughly seven-minute attack on Sand, Vance accused Sand of masquerading as a moderate when he is “far left.” 

“He wants to make sure you hear him groaning about partisanship,” Vance told a crowd of supporters. 

“He’ll say ‘why do we even need labels,’ that’s what he says. But it’s a strange thing to complain about from a guy who has spent his entire life working for and donating to far left, Democratic causes. If partisanship is a problem, and it is, the first place is to look in the damn mirror, Rob, because you’ve been a partisan Democrat your whole life,” he said. 

Vance went on to hit Sand, who is the state’s auditor, on a number of fronts including transgender individuals in women’s sports, abortion, and the Green New Deal, and sought to paint he and other Democratic candidates as extreme. 

“The choice is this simple. It’s common sense versus crazy. It’s a man who listens to you versus a man who looks down on you. It’s a governor who fights for you versus a governor who fights against you,” Vance said. 

“You have an opportunity to not send not just Rob Sand but the entire Democrat Party a message: check the crazy at the door, and learn to fight for Americans for a change,” he continued. 

Polls show a tight gubernatorial race potentially favoring Democrats in the Hawkeye State. A poll released earlier this month from Emerson College Polling/Nexstar Media shows Sand leading his Republican opponent Zach Lahn 49 to 46 percent. 

Vance notably called out Kansas Democratic Senate candidate Adam Hamilton, along with Texas Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico at the rally. The comments come as polls show a tightening Senate race in Kansas. 

While Lahn was present at the rally with Vance, one Iowa candidate who was noticeably absent  was Republican Senate nominee and Rep. Ashley Hinson.

The congresswoman’s Senate campaign said ahead of the rally that she had conflicting events. Hinson is facing a highly competitive race against Iowa State Rep. Josh Turek. The same Emerson College Polling/Nexstar Media survey showed Turek leading Hinson 46 to 44 percent. 

Still, Vance gave Hinson a shoutout. 

“I know she couldn’t be here today, but are we going to elect Ashley Hinson for United States Senator from the great state of Iowa?” the vice president said.

data.title: Anthropic: AI model Claude helping build next version of it
data.description:
Anthropic’s chatbot Claude is leading more than a quarter of the artificial intelligence (AI) firm’s research and development efforts, the company revealed Thursday.

The report marks the latest sign of AI’s growing capabilities within the development space itself, building on months of suggestions from researchers that the technology is getting closer to building and self-improving itself.

As of last month, Claude is “leading” 26 percent of Anthropic’s AI R&D work, a 1 percent jump from last March. Still, Claude is not operating fully autonomously on any measured portion of their work, the company said.

“Frontier AI labs increasingly use AI to build future AI models,” the company wrote in its blog post. “This process allows labs in democratic countries to develop more capable models more quickly and conduct more safety and testing on models before they are released to secure AI’s benefits while staying on the frontier.”

Anthropic also identified about 30,000 AI agents doing research and engineering work at the company at any one time in its internal platform.

It comes just days after Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for a slowdown of the technology’s development in the wake of an ominous warning from a researcher who recently resigned from the firm.

Jacob Coxon, a previously little-known AI researcher who has also worked at OpenAI, went viral on social media last week after claiming researchers at frontier firms “believe AI could kill humans,” but have not slowed development toward superintelligence — a hypothetical AI agent that could outperform all of humanity’s cognitive ability. 

Coxon’s warning was later affirmed by Anthropic’s head of alignment scientist Evan Hubinger, who said, “Jacob is correct here—we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!”

Hubinger said there is a greater than 10 percent chance this occurs within the next decade. 

This camp of researchers believe superintelligence will get to the point where AI will no longer need humans to develop, using instead AI models to duplicate and improve.

Days later, Amodei suggested in his blog that AI companies should collaborate to set standards and agree on a slowdown to address these risks. While lawmakers are scrambling to pass AI safety legislation, they also expressed concerns over the industry trying to self-regulate itself.

data.title: Watch live: Trump to announce Medicaid drug pricing plan
data.description:
President Trump will deliver remarks Friday on another step in his administration’s efforts to lower prescription drug costs.

Trump is expected to announce that Medicaid programs in all 50 states will have access to “most favored nation” pricing for certain drugs. He will be joined by several governors in the Oval Office.

The announcement comes as affordability remains a key issue for voters ahead of the midterm elections.

The event is scheduled to begin at 2:30 p.m. EDT.

Watch live above.

data.title: ICE officer pleads not guilty to lying to FBI about Minneapolis shooting
data.description:
An Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer pleaded not guilty Friday to federal charges stemming from allegations that he lied to authorities about what led up to the January shooting of a Venezuelan man during Minneapolis enforcement operations.

A federal grand jury indicted Christian Castro, 52, in early September on six counts of making materially false statements to investigators. He appeared before a magistrate judge in St. Paul on Friday where he was arraigned on the charges.

Castro, who has reportedly been suspended without pay from the agency, is the first federal immigration officer to be prosecuted by the Justice Department for actions that occurred during Operation Metro Surge in the Twin Cities.

“Mr. Castro voluntarily went to Minneapolis to surrender himself, both in state court and in federal court, and he’s been released on bond, and we look forward to litigating these matters and to presenting our case in court and exonerating him,” Michael Wynn, one of his attorneys, told The Hill.

Castro is accused of lying to the FBI about how a Jan. 14 scuffle with three men, one of whom was shot in the thigh and hospitalized, unfolded.

Officials with the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) initially claimed that an officer, determined to be Castro, fired a “defensive shot” after being attacked with a snow shovel and a broom handle. But court documents indicated that the men had actually dropped the items and ran toward a nearby apartment “as soon as [they] saw his pistol.”

About a month later, DHS said they were investigating what appeared to be “untruthful statements” made by the officer following the review of additional video evidence.

“The men and women of ICE are entrusted with upholding the rule of law and are held to the highest standards of professionalism, integrity, and ethical conduct. Violations of this sacred sworn oath will not be tolerated,” a former spokesperson said at the time.

Friday’s hearing caps off what has been a chaotic few weeks for Castro, who became the center of an extradition fight between Texas Gov. Abbott (R) and Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz (D) after he was jailed in Texas in late May.

Walz accused his counterpart of delay and refusal to sign the paperwork that would have authorized Castro’s transfer so he could face state assault charges in connection with the shooting. A federal judge ultimately declined to intervene, and Castro was released after 90 days.

He was arrested again on Wednesday by Minnesota authorities and made his initial appearance in a state courtroom the next day.

He is currently required to wear a GPS ankle monitor and cannot possess any firearms as part of his bond conditions in the federal case.

data.title: Congress can come together to honor the Adams Family
data.description:
There is plenty that Republicans and Democrats disagree about in Washington. Honoring the extraordinary contributions of the Adams family to the United States should not be one of them.

As the four members of the House of Representatives serving on the Adams Memorial Commission, we represent different parts of the country, different parties, and different political perspectives. But we are united in the belief that John Adams, Abigail Adams, John Quincy Adams, and their remarkable family deserve a permanent memorial in our nation’s capital.

Few American families have contributed as much to the founding, development and preservation of the nation.

John Adams was a leading voice for American independence, a signer of the Declaration of Independence, a diplomat who helped negotiate America’s first international alliance to secure critical financial and military support for the Revolution, and, ultimately, the second president of the United States.

His wife, Abigail, was far more than a witness to that history. During long periods when John was serving the country at home and abroad, she managed their family and farm while becoming one of his most trusted political advisers. Her remarkable correspondence provides an enduring account of the founding era, including her famous appeal to “remember the ladies” at a time when women possessed few political or legal rights.

Their son, John Quincy, carried that tradition of public service into another generation. He served as a diplomat, secretary of State, and the sixth president before returning to public service in the House of Representatives, where he became a fierce opponent of slavery.

And those three lives barely scratch the surface of the Adams family’s contributions to the United States. The family produced generations of diplomats, public servants, writers, and civic leaders whose influence extended far beyond the founding era.

Yet there is still no memorial in Washington honoring this extraordinary American family.

That omission is especially striking as Americans commemorate the 250th anniversary of our independence. John Adams helped make that independence possible. Abigail Adams helped give voice to the principles the new nation would spend generations working to fulfill. Their descendants demonstrated how the responsibilities of citizenship and public service could be passed from one generation to the next.

A memorial to the Adams family would be different from the monuments Washington already knows so well. It would not commemorate only a president, general, or individual achievement. It would tell the story of an American family — men and women, parents and children — bound together across generations by a commitment to public service. The current proposal envisions that memorial near the White House, where John and Abigail became its first residents in 1800.

At a time when Americans hear so much about what divides us, the Adams Memorial offers a small but meaningful reminder of what can still unite us. Republicans and Democrats in the House have already come together unanimously behind this effort.

The Adams family gave generations of service to the country they helped create. Two hundred and fifty years after the Declaration of Independence, it is time for our nation’s capital to give them the recognition they deserve.

The Senate should pass the Adams Memorial-Great American Heroes Act and help make that memorial a reality.

Morgan Griffith, William R. Keating, Stephen F. Lynch and John Moolenaar serve as commissioners on the Adams Memorial Commission.

data.title: JFK's family slams Trump over Kennedy Center: 'How small minded, how narcissistic'
data.description:
The family of former President John F. Kennedy slammed President Trump for his ongoing legal battle to put his name on the Kennedy Center and to close the building planned renovations.

The Kennedy Center board, handpicked by Trump, voted Tuesday to close the main building, but Trump said the renovations will not happen as long as the ruling blocking his name from being added to the center stands.

“If the ruling is a negative one, which it should not be, and is not overturned by the U.S. Supreme Court, the Reconstruction and the Renovation of The Kennedy Center will not take place,” Trump wrote on Truth Social.

JFK’s niece Maria Shriver, who was the former first lady of California, said Trump’s statement “blows my mind,” calling the president “small minded” and “narcissistic.”

“That a sitting president would not let any renovations to a public building go on unless he gets to first put his name in the said building… What a sad state of affairs. What a tragedy,” she wrote on the social platform X.

“It seems that this man will not rest until his name is permanently connected to the name of a great president, whose memory this building was dedicated to,” she added.

JFK’s grandson Jack Schlossberg, who recently ran an unsuccessful campaign in New York’s 12th Congressional District, also weighed in.

“JFK’s legacy is unbreakable — the moon, the Civil Rights Act, Cuban Missile Crisis and the arts. Trump is a broken band in nose dive decline,” he said in a statement.

Rep. Joyce Beatty (D-Ohio), an ex-officio board member, sued in December to block the name change and closure plans. U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper ruled against the board and blocked its attempt to add Trump’s name to the building’s facade.

Kerry Kennedy, the daughter of former Attorney General Robert F. Kennedy, called Beatty a “national hero” for challenging the board and the administration in court.

“She has fiercely and courageously stood up for the Kennedy Center, for the arts, for Uncle Jack’s memory, for this country’s history, and most importantly, for the law, time and time again,” she wrote on social media. “We will not be bullied into silence or submission. Thank you, Rep. Beatty. We are all so grateful for your leadership.”

Her brother, Trump’s Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr., has said in the past that he has “bigger fish to fry” than worrying about a name change.
